extracted.intended_audience: clinicians, healthcare AI researchers, algorithm developers, regulators and healthcare system decision-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for translating machine learning / AI research into safe, effective, and adoptable clinical systems, including evaluation, reporting, deployment, regulation, and human–algorithm interaction considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials as an evidence gold standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials (RCTs) should be viewed as the gold standard for evidence generation for AI systems in healthcare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists examples of RCTs (both positive and negative) and cautions that higher accuracy does not necessarily lead to better patient outcomes. Where possible, future studies should use clinical outcomes as trial endpoints to demonstrate longer-term benefit. Recognises that RCTs may not always be appropriate or feasible and that more sophisticated evaluation approaches may be required when algorithms change care pathways or sociocultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective evaluation (not just retrospective) of AI systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective studies are required to understand real-world utility because retrospective performance may overestimate real-world results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples of limited prospective studies (diabetic retinopathy, polyp detection, wrist fracture detection, congenital cataracts) and notes consumer tech enabling large prospective studies (e.g., Apple Heart Study). Emphasises that performance is likely to deteriorate on data different from training data.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-quality reporting using TRIPOD / TRIPOD-ML standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine learning studies should follow best-practice reporting guidelines such as TRIPOD, and a machine-learning-specific TRIPOD-ML is in development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full and clear reporting of all aspects of a diagnostic or prognostic model is critical to assess risk of bias and usefulness. This includes methodological details necessary to judge validity and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use performance metrics that reflect clinical applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics should aim to capture real clinical applicability and be understandable to intended users; AUC alone is often insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend reporting sensitivity and specificity at selected operating points, positive and negative predictive values, and using multiple measures since no single metric captures all desirable properties. Suggests decision curve analysis to quantify net benefit and emphasises metrics understandable by clinicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clinically meaningful endpoints (patient outcomes, quality of care)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should go beyond technical accuracy to include how AI affects quality of care, variability of healthcare professionals, efficiency, productivity, and patient outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical outcomes are the most important endpoints. The article gives examples where improved technical accuracy did not improve outcomes and stresses trials should aim to use clinical outcomes where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair, objective comparison of algorithms on the same independent test set
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms must be compared on the same independent test set representative of the target population using the same performance metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without common test sets and metrics, fair comparison is impossible. Recommends independent, local, representative test sets constructed from unenriched samples and data not available for training; supplementary local training data can be provided for fine-tuning prior to testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: External validation and representativeness for generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper assessment requires external validation using adequately sized datasets collected from institutions other than the training source to represent real-world variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External validation ensures variation in patient demographics and disease states are represented. Notes that external validation is rare (only 6% in a cited review) and is critical for generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and manage dataset shift (model drift) over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise non-stationary environments and implement methods to identify drift and update models in response to deteriorating performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include periodic quantification of performance, retraining or recalibration, and data-driven procedures to recommend appropriate update methods (from recalibration to full retraining). Periodical testing procedures are suggested for ongoing maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid accidental fitting to confounders rather than true signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure models are not exploiting spurious correlations or confounders present in training datasets that do not reflect causal signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete examples (wolves vs dogs snow/grass; ruler in skin lesion images; scanner model and 'urgent' labels aiding hip fracture detection; portable x-ray machines correlated with pneumonia labels) and calls for ongoing work to understand features learned by networks to improve generalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and mitigate algorithmic bias and fairness issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify algorithmic bias and unfairness and develop mitigations; design algorithms and validations with the intended global community in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distils unfairness into model bias (maj ority-focused), model variance (inadequate minority data), and outcome noise (unobserved interacting variables). Recommends careful performance analysis by subgroups (age, ethnicity, sex, sociodemographic stratum, location), use representative validation populations, and prospective pilots to evaluate benefits and harms if the detected disease spectrum differs from current practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider susceptibility to adversarial attack or manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and evaluate risks that models can be intentionally or unintentionally fooled by adversarial inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples where benign images misclassified by adding adversarial noise or small rotations. Even if mostly theoretical now, adversarial risk should be considered in safety assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reliable measures of model confidence and out-of-distribution detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop methods to detect out-of-distribution inputs and reliable confidence estimates to prevent clinical decisions based on inaccurate outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such measures are important to avoid using models in unfamiliar settings; helps flag when the model should not be trusted or human review is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability and explainability appropriate to clinical use
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems should be trustworthy, transparent, interpretable and explainable, especially when decisions can significantly affect users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues healthcare offers a strong case for explainability (verification, detection of inappropriate reasoning, extraction of scientific insights). Notes a trade-off between performance and explainability, gives approaches (e.g., two-stage segmentation + classification, symbolic techniques, ontologies), and references GDPR right to explanation. Research into explainable AI and evaluation of interpretability is ongoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and evaluate human–algorithm interaction and workflow effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Study how clinicians interact with AI tools, including human performance when assisted by AI and potential negative human behaviours (alert fatigue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples where CAD increased recall without improving outcomes and where human+AI outperformed either alone. Recommends research into human-centred design, interaction effects, and complex evolving relationships in live clinical environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address logistical data availability and interoperability issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that healthcare data are often siloed and difficult to aggregate; adopt unified data formats to improve data availability for machine learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends adoption of standards like FHIR (SMART on FHIR) but warns that improved interoperability may not fix inconsistent semantic coding in EHR data. Data aggregation across imaging, pathology, EHRs, prescribing, and insurance databases is challenging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop regulatory frameworks and post-market surveillance
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation must balance pace of innovation with potential for harm, and include thoughtful post-market surveillance to protect patients and enable beneficial innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References FDA proposed framework for AI/ML-based SaMD, and highlights need for proactive regulation to give clinicians confidence. Post-market monitoring should identify performance deficits over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for model updates and continuous learning in regulation and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the regulatory impact of product improvements and upgrades; prefer periodic system-wide updates following full clinical-evaluation over continuous uncontrolled updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous learning poses challenges to traditional evaluation processes. Recommends ongoing performance monitoring guidelines, calibration using human feedback, and evaluated update policies to manage drift and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use open datasets and common benchmarks to facilitate reproducible comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of large, open datasets allows consistent benchmarking and easier algorithm comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages use of open data for researchers to benchmark performance, alongside local independent test sets for deployment-specific assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report model operating points and predictive values clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the chosen operating point(s) and corresponding sensitivity/specificity as well as positive and negative predictive values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turning continuous model outputs into discrete decision categories requires a reported operating point; PPV/NPV help clinicians understand real-world utility. Notes that no single measure suffices and multiple metrics should be presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform prospective pilots and local testing before broad deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct prospective pilots within healthcare systems to understand product characteristics, pitfalls in practical deployment, and local effects before scaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilots help detect practical issues such as differences in disease spectrum, workflow impacts, bias, or unintended harms and inform necessary mitigations or adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate clinicians and students to appraise and use AI safely
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accessible AI curriculum for medical students and practising clinicians to enable critical appraisal, adoption, and safe use of AI tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improving clinicians' understanding of AI will support appropriate adoption and enable clinicians to participate in system design, bias quantification, and interpretation of results.
